extracted.intended_audience: members/readers of the Royal Society; natural philosophers and practicing scientists (17th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply substantive evaluative principles, methods, and practical guidance embedded in 17th-century natural philosophy journal articles (physiology, meteorology, geology, acoustics, navigational tables). Focus on how authors justify inferences, prescribe observational/experimental methods, and give practical instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative anatomy plus experimental manipulation to infer organ function
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer the function of an organ by purposely examining that organ across many kinds of animals and, where appropriate, performing manipulative experiments (e.g., tying up the caecum) to test physiological consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lister reports examining intestines of many animals to discern patterns (correlating caecum size with 'figured' excrements) and suggests experimental intervention (tying the caecum) to see if diarrhea results — treating comparative observation and direct experiment as complementary evidence for functional hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anatomical correlation as evidence for physiological role
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correlations between anatomical form/size and observed physiological/behavioral features (e.g., large caecum in animals that void consistently figured excrements) as evidence toward hypothesized function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lister argues that a capacious caecum in animals that produce uniformly-shaped droppings supports the caecum's role in 'draining, baking, hardened' the excrements to receive figure; absence or small caecum in naturally loose animals is used as corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate multiple plausible functional ends and weigh them
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing an organ's use, list and weigh several possible purposes (preventing diarrhoea, aiding survival during hunger, enhancing digestion/fermentation) rather than a single definitive claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lister offers three possible ends for the caecum's figuration of excrements and discusses their plausibility, demonstrating a standard of offering multiple explanatory hypotheses grounded in observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical directions for using tide tables with local adjustment factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying a general tide table to local ports, adjust times according to local conditions (add or subtract specified hours/minutes per location) and account for climatic or wind-driven deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed advises users to note effects of droughts/frosts and prevailing winds (N or N.W. tending to lengthen tides, opposite winds and heavy rains shortening them), states the typical discrepancy ('very rarely... more than half an hour'), and provides an explicit add/subtract table of h:m adjustments for named ports to adapt the Thames-based table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use seamen's experiential knowledge to validate and adapt tidal theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement theoretical tide calculations by inquiry among experienced seamen to ensure correspondence with observed high waters at local ports, and incorporate that empirical knowledge into practical reduction tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flamsteed reports consulting 'our most experienced seamen' and using their reports to make a reduction table so the tide table 'may be made to serve' at enumerated places; this treats practitioner testimony as valid calibration data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for identifying in-situ petrifactions versus transported shells
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret 'formed stones' (conchites/petrifactions) as mineral casts (not transported shell remains) when found: (a) in an undisturbed geological layer, (b) with both imperfect and complete forms indicating progressive formation, (c) filled with local marl/earth, (d) showing chemical reactions (e.g., effervescence in vinegar) and (e) lacking closed valves or animal-exuviae structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hatley notes that the occurrences in a never-before-disturbed ground, presence of specimens 'in fieri' (stages toward complete formation), internal filling matching marl, and behaviors under boiling/washing/acid strongly argue for being lapides sui generis; the text uses these lines of evidence as a checklist for interpreting unusual fossils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gradational/imperfection evidence to argue in-situ formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the presence of specimens at varying states of completion (from prima stamina to fully formed) as an 'unanswerable argument' against their being remnants of animals, and as positive evidence of mineral-formative processes in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reasons that imperfect as well as complete formations, and occurrence in undisturbed strata, indicate progressive mineral deposition forming shell-like figures rather than transported detritus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify hearing analogous to vision: direct, refracted, reflected
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide hearing into three analogous modalities — direct, refracted, and reflected hearing — and correspondingly subdivide the study into acoustics, diacoustics (refracted), and catacoustics (reflected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bishop of Ferns frames a conceptual taxonomy mirroring optics, proposing new branch names (otacoustics/diacoustics/catacoustics or phonics/diaphonics/cataphonics) to structure the science of sound and its improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve sound production and propagation by controlling object placement and medium
rubrics_metrics.description: To improve the propagation of sound, attend both to the sonorous object's positioning (near smooth walls/arches, near water) and to the medium's condition (thin, quiescent air, still nights) because these factors materially affect how far and how distinctly sound travels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: placing a sound near a smooth plane or arched wall enhances rolling and consolidation of sound (explains whispering galleries); sounds near water are conveyed farther and more softly; in plains and still nights sounds travel farther than over uneven ground or turbulent air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve reception by positioning the ear and designing acoustic architectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Reception can be improved by placing the ear near the propagation surface (wall, water, ground) or by designing spaces (arches, whispering places) that direct and consolidate sound to listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that listeners at the far end of a church can hear better by leaning their ears close to the wall; laying an ear close to the ground in a plain at night greatly extends hearing range — implying practical listening techniques and architectural design principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical design principle: apply optical instrument concepts to acoustics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use analogies from optical instruments (spectacles, telescopes, microscopes, polyscopes) to guide the invention of acoustic instruments (otacoustics: hearing-aiding tubes; microphones/micracoustics: magnifying ears; polyphones/polyacoustics: multiplying a sound to simulate many instruments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bishop argues that just as spectacles/telescopes/microscopes extend vision, corresponding acoustic devices could amplify distant or minute sounds, render single sounds as many, or create 'true harmony' by multiplying sounds — a methodological prescription for instrument development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize medium-induced alteration of perceived sound (refracted hearing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that variations in medium density, figure, magnitude and incidence alter how sound is perceived (refracted hearing), analogous to refracted vision; such effects must be considered when interpreting acoustic phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains that thickened air can materially change the character of perceived sound and that instruments might be devised both to strengthen the sonorous body and to help the ear receive and discern refracted sounds.
